White’s 1. b3 is a quiet, preparatory move: it intends Bb2 and puts the bishop on the long diagonal, but it creates no immediate tactical threat. Black should take the center while developing naturally. Playing 1...e5 grabs central space and opens good lines for Black’s pieces. If White continues 2.Bb2, Black can answer 2...Nc6, defending the e5-pawn while developing; White cannot grab the pawn cheaply. Black can follow up with Nf6, d6, Bc5/Be7, and castling.

Move: e5

Black has just placed a pawn on e5, gaining central space, but that pawn is not yet defended. Developing the queen’s bishop to b2 puts immediate pressure on e5 along the long diagonal and fits naturally with the b3 setup. This also avoids giving Black the tempo of ...e4 against a knight on f3. White can follow up with e3, Nf3, Be2, and castling, maintaining a flexible center and pressure on Black’s position.

Move: Bb2

White has just developed the bishop to b2, and it immediately attacks Black’s e5 pawn. Black should meet this threat with a natural developing move that also reinforces the center.

2...Nc6 develops a knight to a strong square and gives the e5 pawn protection. If White tries 3.Bxe5, then 3...Nxe5 wins the bishop for only a pawn, so White won’t want to take. The knight also supports central pawn advances and Black can follow up with moves like ...Nf6, ...d6, and ...Bc5.

Move: Nc6
